questions.question: What is a pull request (PR) and why is it used?
questions.title: What Is a Pull Request?
questions.direct_answer: A pull request is a mechanism on hosting platforms like GitHub/GitLab to propose merging a feature branch into another branch, enabling code review, discussion, and automated checks before the merge happens.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of professional team collaboration workflows — PRs are the gatekeeping mechanism for production code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing a PR purely as a technical merge operation without mentioning the human/review process
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that PR descriptions and linked issues are part of project documentation and audit trail

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A pull request — or PR — is a feature of Git hosting platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket. It's not a Git command itself, but a collaborative workflow layer on top of Git. When you've finished working on a feature branch and you want it merged into main, you open a PR. You're essentially saying 'I've made these changes, please review them and if they look good, merge them.' The PR creates a space for discussion — team members can review the code line by line, leave comments, suggest changes, and ask questions. You can push additional commits to address feedback, and the PR automatically updates. Automated checks — CI tests, code coverage, linting — also run against the PR. Only when reviewers approve and checks pass does the code get merged. Beyond the immediate technical function, PRs serve as a permanent record of why a change was made, what was discussed, and who approved it. A well-written PR description is part of the project's history and helps future engineers understand context.

sections.title: Key Points
content: PR = request to merge a feature branch into main (or another target branch)
Not a Git command — a feature of GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket layered on top of Git
Enables code review: line-by-line comments, change requests, approval workflow
CI/CD integration: automated tests run on the PR before merge
PRs are also documentation — they explain 'why' a change was made and record the review discussion

questions.question: What are the different merge strategies available when merging a pull request on GitHub?
questions.title: PR Merge Strategies: Merge, Squash, Rebase
questions.direct_answer: GitHub offers three strategies: 'Merge commit' (creates a merge commit preserving all history), 'Squash and merge' (combines all PR commits into one), and 'Rebase and merge' (replays commits linearly without a merge commit).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical workflow knowledge — this comes up in daily work discussions and team code review practices
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing 'merge' exists — not knowing squash is the most popular choice for keeping main history clean
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which strategy suits which team — squash for clean main, rebase for linear history purists, merge for full auditability

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When merging a PR on GitHub, you have three choices. 'Create a merge commit' is the standard git merge — it preserves all your feature branch commits and adds a merge commit. The main branch history shows all the granular WIP commits like 'fix typo', 'add test', 'address review comment'. This gives complete history but can make the log cluttered. 'Squash and merge' is probably the most popular choice — it takes all your PR's commits, regardless of how many, and squashes them into a single commit on main. Main gets one clean, well-described commit per feature. Your individual WIP commits disappear. This keeps the main branch history very readable — one commit per feature or fix. 'Rebase and merge' replays each of your commits individually onto main without a merge commit, giving a linear history. The catch: commit timestamps and authors are preserved but SHAs change, and you lose the explicit record of which commits came from a PR. Most teams that care about clean history go with squash and merge because it's the best balance between clean main history and easy reversion.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Merge commit: preserves all commits + creates merge commit — full history, can be noisy
Squash and merge: all PR commits → one commit on main — cleanest main branch log
Rebase and merge: replays each commit linearly, no merge commit — linear but no PR grouping visible
Most teams prefer squash and merge for keeping main clean and readable
Team convention matters — pick one and be consistent

questions.question: What should you include in a pull request to make it easy to review?
questions.title: Pull Request Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: A good PR has a clear description explaining what changed and why, linked issue, small focused scope, passing tests, and screenshots or examples where relevant — making the reviewer's job easy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Professional habits and empathy for reviewers — shows the candidate understands team dynamics
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Opening a 2000-line PR with no description — this is a common junior developer habit that frustrates teams
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention self-reviewing your own PR before requesting review — catching your own issues first

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A good pull request is one that a reviewer can understand quickly and review confidently. The description should explain what you changed and why — not just 'fixed bug' but 'Fixed NPE in UserService when email is null. Added null check in validateUser() and unit test covering this case. Resolves #123.' Link the relevant issue or ticket so the reviewer has context. Keep PRs small and focused — a PR should do one thing. If you find yourself saying 'also while I was in there I refactored...' — that belongs in a separate PR. Before requesting review, do a self-review: read every line of your own diff, check that you haven't left debug logs or TODO comments, and verify all tests pass. If there's UI change, add screenshots. If there's an API change, show example request/response. The easier you make it for the reviewer, the faster you'll get feedback, and the better the collaboration culture. Large unfocused PRs with no description are one of the quickest ways to frustrate experienced teammates.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Clear description: what changed, why, how to test it
Link to relevant issue or ticket
Keep PRs small and focused — one feature or fix per PR
Ensure all CI checks pass before requesting review
Self-review first: read your own diff, remove debug logs, verify tests pass

questions.question: What is a draft pull request and when would you use it?
questions.title: Draft Pull Requests
questions.direct_answer: A draft PR signals that the work is still in progress and not ready for formal review — it enables early feedback, visibility to the team, and CI checks without requesting a full review.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of collaboration features and good team communication habits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing draft PRs exist and instead opening a PR with a title like 'WIP: don't merge'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that draft PRs are great for getting early architectural feedback before investing in a full implementation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A draft pull request is a way to say 'I'm sharing my work-in-progress with the team, but I'm not asking for a formal review yet.' On GitHub, you open a draft PR and it's clearly marked as a draft — reviewers can see it, CI runs against it, but they know it's not ready for a full code review and they won't be pinged. There are several good reasons to use draft PRs. First, early feedback: you've written the skeleton of an approach and want your tech lead to sanity-check the direction before you build out all the details. Second, CI visibility: your tests run on every push, so you can see failures early even before the work is complete. Third, team awareness: your teammates can see what you're working on without feeling obligated to review yet. Fourth, it's better than the 'WIP:' title prefix hack. Once you're ready for review, you just click 'Ready for review' and it converts to a normal PR and notifies reviewers.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Draft PR = work in progress, explicitly not ready for formal review
CI still runs, team can see progress, but no formal review requested
Good for early architectural feedback before full implementation
Prevents reviewers from wasting time on incomplete work
Convert to ready: click 'Ready for review' button — notifies assigned reviewers

questions.question: How do you address review comments on a pull request?
questions.title: Addressing Pull Request Review Comments
questions.direct_answer: Address review comments by making the requested code changes, committing them to the same branch, which automatically updates the PR — then respond to each comment explaining what you changed or why you disagree.

interviewer_intent.testing: Communication skills and professional collaboration etiquette during code review
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Ignoring comments, or just pushing changes without explaining what you did — leaving the reviewer to re-read everything
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that code review is a conversation, not a verdict — it's okay to respectfully disagree and discuss

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a reviewer leaves comments on your PR, here's the professional approach. First, read all the feedback before jumping to make changes — you want to understand the full picture. For each comment: if you agree, make the change, commit it to the same branch (the PR automatically updates), and reply to the comment with something like 'Done — refactored as suggested' or 'Fixed in commit abc123.' This closes the loop for the reviewer. If you disagree with a comment, don't just ignore it — reply with your reasoning. Maybe the reviewer missed some context, or maybe you genuinely have a different design preference. It's a conversation. Say something like 'I see the concern about performance, but this code path is called once at startup, so the overhead is negligible — thoughts?' Good engineers welcome this kind of discussion. Once you've addressed everything, ping the reviewer or re-request review. Avoid force-pushing during active review — it makes it hard for reviewers to see what changed. Add new commits instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Make changes on the same branch — the PR auto-updates with new commits
Reply to each comment explaining what you changed (close the loop for reviewers)
For disagreements: discuss respectfully with reasoning, don't just ignore
Avoid force-pushing during active review — add new commits so reviewers see incremental changes
Re-request review once all comments are addressed
